newsitem.title: USA: Dlr closes weaker, near day lows in thin US trade.
newsitem.headline: Dlr closes weaker, near day lows in thin US trade.

text.p: The dollar slumped in the U.S. as short-term speculators pushed dollar/mark through sell stops in thin holiday trading, dealers said.

The greenback had fallen overnight against the yen as comments by Japanese Ministry of Finance official Eisuke Sakakibara failed to reverse market perceptions that Japan has abandoned its ostensible weak-yen, strong-dollar campaign.

Light volume allowed day traders to move the dollar past stops near 1.4990 and 1.4960 marks, ultimately stretching all the way to 1.4910 marks, the lowest point since 1.4880 marks on September 9, by early afternoon.

"With the lack of liquidity and a lot of junior people manning the desks, stops become very attractive targets for interbank dealers looking to get things going," said James Powers, vice president at Westdeutsche Landesbank Girozentrale in New York.
At the 1300 ET/1800 GMT close of IMM trading, the dollar stood at 1.4945/55 marks, down from 1.5045/50 at Friday's close. The greenback also fell to 110.90/00 yen, down from 111.70/75 Friday.
Trading in the U.S. ended early because of the Veterans Day holiday. Holidays also closed some bourses in Europe.
Sterling also slumped against the mark, which may have hurt dollar/mark as well. Sterling/mark fell over two pfennigs to the 2.4650 area from the day's high at 2.4905.
"It's possible an order to sell sterling/mark in a thin market had a larger-than-usual impact," said Tom Hoge, corporate trader at Bank of New York.
Dealers noted the break of psychologically important support at 1.50 marks could portend larger losses ahead.
"I think it is just a matter of time until we have a follow-through of consolidation, maybe 1.4850 (marks)," said Russ Lascala, head of spot currency trading at Citibank.
The dollar continues to suffer from fallout over Sakakibara's comments last Thursday that hinted at a near-term cap for dollar/yen, traders said.
Early Monday, Sakakibara said Japan's foreign exchange policy was unchanged, but that failed to shake market players' belief that Japan has tempered its longstanding support for the dollar.
"We are seeing repercussions from Sakakibara's non-denial of his statements the other night," said Lascala.

"Everyone was waiting for a flat-out denial and it never happened. We're concluding that this is exactly what the Japanese wanted to happen -- dollar/yen consolidation back to the 105 to 112 area," Lascala added.
In other trade, the dollar fell to 1.2570/80 Swiss francs from 1.2640/50 at Friday's close. Sterling dipped to $1.6470/80 from $1.6478/88 on Friday.
The dollar stood at Canadian $1.3341/46 and the Australian dollar stood at $0.7866/71 Monday afternoon.
